name: Carla Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and lead a dragline crew at a large mine. I have a two-year technical diploma and can tell from the cable sound when a heavy bucket is sitting badly. I teach the younger operators the hand signals and still check each cable before a lift. My title is senior, but the pay is low here and recent short shifts have left us with less than a month saved.

say: I accept a **quicker sheet** if a person still inspects the dragline cable.
I trust **direct checks** before starting the bucket.
think: I am relieved by **small AI change**, but current pay barely covers bills.
I have **less than one month** saved despite years on the machine.
do: **Keep** taking dragline shifts and using the cable checklist.
**Compare** rosters with payslips and pay electricity arrears from extra shifts if paid.
feel: **Anxious** about household bills rather than the mild technology change.
S0.quote: My years operating the mine's dragline do not make the electricity bill wait.
fieldNote: **Senior standing** sits beside a lower rate and less than a month saved.
**Resistant adoption** is consistent: she will read required sheets but keeps physical cable checks.

steps.text: Keep taking dragline shifts and using the cable checklist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the dragline crew that a quicker daily sheet is all right, but a screen cannot see a worn cable by itself. I have never used AI and still check the line and bucket with my own eyes before we start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would welcome a quiet technology year, but the household budget is tight already. I am a senior operator on a lower rate than the title sounds, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. If one shift is lost, my partner and I have to move a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking dragline shifts and use the same cable checklist. In the first year I would compare each roster with the payslip and put any paid extra shift toward the electricity arrears before buying anything optional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our pay, even though the machine change is small. My years operating the mine's dragline do not make the electricity bill wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the arrears start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We had a run of short shifts when a machine was repaired, and the bill carried over. I would rather clear it from work than ask our grown children to pay it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an automatic sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read it if the supervisor required it and check every cable entry myself. I would not trust a neat box more than the wire in front of me.

say: I expect **buying and scheduling** to change before dragline operation.
I want a **full ground trial** before the mine changes crew numbers.
think: I think **office jobs** change first and junior helpers may be exposed later.
I cannot ignore **small hour cuts** with less than a month saved.
do: **Record** every lost shift in my pay book.
**Wait** for a full ground trial before accepting a changed crew pattern.
feel: **Anxious** about small pay cuts while regular physical shifts appear safe for now.
S1.quote: A glossy video will not tell me whether a real shift can run safely.
fieldNote: **Trial demand** is hands-on: wet ground, a heavy load and a snag to clear.
**Trainee loyalty** shapes her concern about slower robot adoption reducing helpers first.
**Thin cushion** keeps her anxious even when her senior dragline work seems secure now.

steps.text: Keep the current dragline rota while office tasks change
Wait for a wet-ground robot trial before accepting a changed rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can speed up buying and scheduling, but a dragline crew still needs to judge the cable and ground. The mine should show us a working machine before using robot plans to change the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may lose work first. Robots spread into hands-on jobs more slowly, so I expect regular dragline shifts for a while, but a junior helper may go if staffing tightens. I would watch my own pay closely because our cushion is so thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current rota and ask the foreman for written trial dates when a robot test is planned. In the first year I would record every lost shift in my pay book and wait for a full ground trial before accepting a new crew pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household account, although the physical job looks safe near term. A small hours cut would land before any grand change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a ground trial need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch the cable lift a heavy load after rain and see who clears a snag. A glossy video will not tell me whether a real shift can run safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which helper worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My trainee coworker Ivo has finally learned the cable signals. I would tell him what the foreman says about staffing, and I would not call a rumour a decision.

say: I separate **2028 scheduling** from dragline robots around 2031.
I want **written staffing estimates** before assuming senior operators keep every shift.
think: I expect **large crew cuts** if robots handle cable work, and my pay could fall.
I cannot cover a long gap with **less than one month** saved and few local jobs.
do: **Request** written staffing estimates and a pension statement now.
**Apply** for nearby dragline posts if my shifts fall after 2028.
**Cut** optional phone and television costs to protect rent and power.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major cuts and sleepless worry about household bills.
S2.quote: I lie awake working out how long the household could last if half my shifts vanished.
fieldNote: **Age 63** at robot arrival comes before any retirement income she has verified.
**Physical risk** arrives with robots around 2031, not with 2028 office scheduling change.
**Private courses** are rejected because the household cannot fund one without a real job.

steps.text: Apply for nearby dragline posts if shifts fall after 2028
Cut optional phone and television costs to protect essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI takes scheduling by 2028, while capable dragline robots come around 2031. We should ask the foreman what the actual roster will look like before anyone calls a senior operator safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the robots arrive. I expect the mine to cut many dragline crew shifts if the robot handles cable work, and mine could be among them. We have less than a month saved and few similar jobs nearby, so losing a big share of pay would put bills behind quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the foreman now for written staffing estimates and check my pension statement. In the first year after 2028 I would apply for any open dragline post at the nearby mines if my shifts fall, and cut the optional phone and television costs to protect rent and power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I lie awake working out how long the household could last if half my shifts vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children the truth, but they have homes of their own. If we had a shortfall, I would first ask my partner what expenses we can cut together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you take a control course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would consider paid instruction on a machine the mine has tested, if there is a real job at the end. I would not spend our last few weeks of money on a private certificate.

say: I see **2031 planning** change before dragline robots around 2034.
I want **honest shift numbers** and apprenticeships with paid time.
think: I might retire at **66** only if pension income covers ordinary bills.
I could need **mine wages** when local openings are scarce.
do: **Request** a pension estimate and compare it with rent and power.
**Keep** driving dragline shifts after 2031 while wages are needed.
**Take** paid robot instruction if a tested machine and continuing work are offered.
feel: **Anxious** about needing wages at 66, with time to check the pension.
S3.quote: I would not count a possible opening as pay until someone offered it.
fieldNote: **Age 66** at capable robots is not an automatic retirement date with a thin cushion.
**Paid instruction** depends on a tested machine and a continuing job.
**Local scarcity** limits her fallback despite senior experience.

steps.text: Keep driving paid dragline shifts while the pension is checked
Take paid robot instruction if tested equipment and work are offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI changes planning by 2031, and capable dragline robots arrive around 2034. A few extra years should be used for honest shift numbers and apprenticeships people can actually attend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 at the robot date. I might be able to retire then, but less than a month saved tells me not to guess at the pension. If I still need wages, a robot roster could leave me looking for work when local openings are scarce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a pension estimate this year and compare it with our rent and power bills. In the first year after 2031 I would keep my dragline shifts and take paid instruction on a tested robot only if the mine offers a place tied to continuing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though the extra years give me time to check the pension. I do not want to be pushed into a course with no wages attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension is enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would check whether the monthly amount still covers medicine and food after rent. If it does, I could choose fewer shifts before a robot arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if it is short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep driving and ask the foreman about any existing cable-inspection work. I would not count a possible opening as pay until someone offered it.

say: I separate **2036 plans** from capable dragline robots around 2039.
I want **pension and staffing** facts while the mine still has time to act.
think: I hope to retire before **71**, but our thin savings make that uncertain.
I might need **paid shifts** before robots arrive if the pension is short.
do: **Keep** safe dragline shifts while they pay household bills.
**Check** yearly pension statements with my partner.
**Seek** nearby part-time equipment-check work if pension income falls short.
feel: **Anxious** about bills and retirement income despite the distant robot date.
S4.quote: I would rather earn what I can while I can still inspect a cable safely.
fieldNote: **Age 68** at thinking AI and 71 at robots makes retirement income her first concern.
**Electricity arrears** and less than a month saved keep financial anxiety present even in the long scenario.
**Nearby workshop work** is a possible application, not a guaranteed vacancy.

steps.text: Keep safe paid dragline shifts while needed
Seek nearby part-time cable-inspection work if pension income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI changes plans around 2036 and capable dragline robots follow around 2039. The mine has plenty of warning to tell workers the truth about pensions and staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the thinking date and 71 when robots arrive. I hope to be retired before then, but the electricity arrears and thin savings today keep me cautious. If the pension is short, I may need more paid shifts before robots ever come to the cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working safe dragline shifts and ask for a pension statement each year. In the first year after 2036 I would check the statement with my partner, then seek a nearby part-time equipment-check job if the pension leaves a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bills more than about the distant robot. Ten years is useful only if we use the pay to catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What nearby work would you seek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mine workshop whether it needs someone to inspect cables on short shifts. I know the work and could reach the workshop from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would listen if our children offered, but I would not build retirement on their wages. I would rather earn what I can while I can still inspect a cable safely.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable dragline robots around 2031 could take a large share of my shifts at 63. Written staffing estimates and a real pension statement would help us decide whether to keep looking for work. I would consider paid instruction only if the mine had tested the equipment and offered continuing work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the electricity when an experienced operator loses a shift. Skill cannot be deposited into the household account until the mine pays for work.

headlineQuote: Skill cannot be deposited into the household account until the mine pays for work.
portrait: **Carla, 58**, leads a dragline crew and checks cable sound and hand signals before every lift.
**Low pay** and less than a month saved leave her household exposed despite senior skill and a technical diploma.
**Familiar checks** guide her; she never uses AI and considers new controls only after paid, proven instruction.
**Fast AGI** alarms her because 2028 scheduling change may precede large dragline cuts around 2031.
**Longer warning** gives her time to verify pension income, but electricity arrears keep financial worry alive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut senior dragline shifts around 2031 while her household has almost no reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing estimates** and a pension statement would let her judge wages against retirement.
**Paid proven instruction** tied to continuing work would give her a possible route if the mine changes equipment.
